content: Soybean oil-based lipid emulsions (S-LE), which are traditionally used in parenteral nutrition (PN) for preterm infants, contain high levels of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) and phytosterols. These components may contribute to adverse effects in this vulnerable population. Recently, newer lipid emulsions (LEs) derived from alternative lipid sources have become available for use in preterm infants. The objective of this review was to evaluate the safety and efficacy of various lipid emulsions used in PN for preterm infants born before 37 weeks of gestation. This included preterm infants with surgical conditions or those with parenteral nutrition-associated liver disease (PNALD) or cholestasis. The analysis involved direct comparisons and pairwise meta-analyses of different LEs. The review included 29 studies with a total of 2,037 participants. The lipid emulsions were categorized into three main groups: (1) fish oil-containing LEs, which included pure fish oil LEs (F-LE) and multisource LEs (e.g., medium-chain triglycerides (MCT)-olive-fish-soybean oil LEs (MOFS-LE), MCT-fish-soybean oil LEs (MFS-LE), and olive-fish-soybean oil LEs (OFS-LE)); (2) conventional soybean oil-based LEs (S-LE); and (3) alternative LEs, such as MCT-soybean oil LEs (MS-LE), olive-soybean oil LEs, and borage oil-based LEs. The primary outcome of interest was the incidence of PNALD or cholestasis, defined as a conjugated bilirubin (Cbil) level of 2 mg/dL or greater. Resolution of PNALD/cholestasis was defined as a Cbil level below 2 mg/dL. However, the included studies used varying definitions of PNALD, with Cbil cutoffs ranging from 1 mg/dL (17.1 μmol/L) to 3 mg/dL (50 μmol/L). In preterm infants, meta-analysis revealed no significant difference in the incidence of PNALD/cholestasis (Cbil cutoff: 2 mg/dL) between fish oil-containing LEs and non-fish oil LEs (risk ratio (RR) 0.61, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.24 to 1.56; risk difference (RD) -0.03, 95% CI -0.08 to 0.02; 4 studies; n = 328; low-quality evidence). When considering any definition of PNALD (with varying Cbil cutoffs), meta-analysis also showed no significant difference between fish oil LEs and non-fish oil LEs (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.21; RD -0.02, 95% CI -0.05 to 0.02; 10 studies; n = 1,024; low-quality evidence). Subgroup analyses of individual LE types did not reveal any significant differences in outcomes. In preterm infants with surgical conditions or cholestasis, only one small study each was available. These studies reported no significant differences in the incidence or resolution of cholestasis when comparing pure fish oil LEs to S-LEs (using a Cbil cutoff of 2 mg/dL). However, in preterm infants with PNALD/cholestasis (using any definition), meta-analysis indicated significantly less cholestasis with fish oil LEs compared to S-LEs (RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.91; RD -0.39, 95% CI -0.65 to -0.12; number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB) 3, 95% CI 2 to 9; 2 studies; n = 40; very low-quality evidence). It is important to note that this finding was based on a very small number of participants from two studies with methodological differences, one of which was terminated early, leading to uncertainty in the effect estimates. Regarding growth outcomes in preterm infants, no differences were observed between LE types in pairwise meta-analyses. There was a lack of sufficient studies in preterm infants with surgical conditions or cholestasis to perform meta-analyses for growth and most other outcomes. For secondary outcomes, meta-analysis showed no significant differences between fish oil LEs and non-fish oil LEs in the incidence of severe retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) (stage 3 or greater, or requiring surgery: RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.16; RD -0.03, 95% CI -0.07 to 0.02; 7 studies; n = 731; very low-quality evidence). Similarly, no differences were found between LE types in pairwise meta-analyses for other outcomes, including mortality, bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), duration of ventilation, patent ductus arteriosus, sepsis, necrotizing enterocolitis, intraventricular hemorrhage, periventricular leukomalacia, jaundice, hyperglycemia, hypertriglyceridemia, intrahepatocellular lipid content, and conjugated bilirubin levels. In surgical infants, one study (n = 19) reported no significant differences in mortality, sepsis rates, Cbil levels, or neurodevelopmental outcomes when comparing pure fish oil LEs to S-LEs. In infants with cholestasis, meta-analyses showed no significant differences in mortality or sepsis rates between fish oil LEs and S-LEs (2 studies; n = 40; very low-quality evidence). In conclusion, this review did not identify any specific lipid emulsion, with or without fish oil, as superior to others in preventing PNALD/cholestasis, promoting growth, or improving other neonatal outcomes in preterm infants. For preterm infants with surgical conditions or cholestasis, there is currently insufficient evidence from randomized studies to determine whether fish oil-containing LEs offer any advantage in preventing or resolving cholestasis or improving other clinical outcomes. Further research, including larger and well-designed trials, is needed to determine the optimal composition of lipid emulsions for preterm infants and to evaluate the role of fish oil-containing and other LEs in preventing and managing PNALD, ROP, and other clinical outcomes.
